item.title: Netherlands narrowly beat Serbia in Nations League
item.description:
Netherlands narrowly beat Serbia in Nations League

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands men’s football team beat Serbia 2-1 in the Nations League in Eindhoven on Sunday, marking Xavi Hernández’s second win in four games as head coach.

Substitute Joshua Zirkzee scored the winning goal in the 71st minute in a game that also marked captain Virgil van Dijk’s 100th cap, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Teun Koopmeiners put the home side ahead in the first half with a free kick. Serbia equalised soon afterwards by a goal from 19-year-old Anderlecht striker Mihajlo Cvetkovic.

Zirkzee tapped in the winner from close range after Crysencio Summerville’s cross was laid back by Tijjani Reijnders. The Dutch finished with 10 men after Micky van de Ven went off with a hand injury, as Xavi had already used all his substitutes.

Xavi, who was appointed in August, has now won twice and drawn twice in his first four games. Germany and Greece drew 0-0 on Sunday, which leaves the Netherlands joint top of their group.

The next round of international matches is in November.

item.title: Sudanese-Dutch lawyer made minister of paramilitary group
item.description:
Sudanese-Dutch lawyer made minister of paramilitary group

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A man with dual Sudanese and Dutch nationality has been named the minister of justice for the controversial Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group attempting to seize power in Sudan.

Osama Said, a lawyer based in the Netherlands, told broadcaster NOS he wanted to bring peace to the war-torn country. He is working in politics “with one goal: to alleviate the suffering of the Sudanese,” he said.

Some 60,000 people have been killed and more than 13 million displaced since fighting broke out in 2023 between the Rapid Support Forces and the government-backed Sudanese Armed Forces, according to the United Nations.

The RSF has set up an alternative government, which is not recognised by the Netherlands and has been designated a terrorist organisation by the European Union.

According to the UN, the RSF engaged in an 18-month siege of the city of El Fasher in the western Darfur region, cutting off food and medical supplies. Civilians who fled were massacred, subjected to sexual violence and forced into servitude, Amnesty International said in a July report.

item.title: Hans Anders to stop selling camera glasses over privacy concerns
item.description:
Hans Anders to stop selling camera glasses over privacy concerns

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Eyewear chain Hans Anders will stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

Victim advocacy group Offlimits says it is helping hundreds of women who have been filmed without their consent, many of whom have seen those images distributed online or through social media groups.

“Hiding a camera in an everyday object facilitates transgressive online behaviour,” the organisation’s director Robbert Hoving said in a statement. They are calling on Meta to stop selling the eyewear, and said they would take the tech giant to court if sales were not halted.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP warned last week that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR rules unless permission is given by everyone in the image.

Last month, the consumer watchdog Consumentenbond issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a board measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.

Last week, Instagram removed a video by Roel Maalderink in which the satirical journalist films himself asking the employees of parent company Meta how they feel about the controversial camera glasses.

item.title: Total student debt falls for the first time, to €28 billion
item.description:
Total student debt falls for the first time, to €28 billion

October 5, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The total amount of student loans owed in the Netherlands has fallen for the first time, according to national statistics office CBS.

Students and former students owed €28 billion at the start of 2026 – €800 million less than a year earlier. The fall is due to fewer students taking out loans since the basic grant was reinstated for higher education students in the 2023-2024 academic year.

The grant was scrapped in 2015 and replaced with a loan system, leaving a generation of students to borrow to cover their living costs.

Some 1.5 million people had student debts in January, a figure that has now fallen for three years running. The number of current students with a loan has dropped to around 400,000, down 210,000 since 2023.

The number of former students with debt is still rising, but more slowly. It went up by just over 6,000 this year, compared with 28,000 a year earlier, and now stands at more than 1.1 million.

People owing large debts are also more common. Some 145,000 people owe €50,000 or more, twice as many as six years ago, and almost 5,000 owe at least €100,000. At the other end of the scale, almost half of all borrowers owe less than €10,000.

The average debt has risen by €5,900 since the loan system was introduced, to €18,300. Current students owe €15,600 on average, €1,000 less than last year, while former students owe an average of €19,200.

item.title: Fries with that? Homes near Amsterdam TikTok queue sell for less
item.description:
Fries with that? Homes near Amsterdam TikTok queue sell for less

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Homes near Fabel Friet, an Amsterdam chip shop whose TikTok-fuelled queues have become one of the city’s more unlikely tourist attractions, sell for less than comparable homes just streets away, according to a TU Delft study.

The research, reported by local broadcaster AT5, came out this week at the same time as the city council and the shop’s owners faced off in court over the queue and how to deal with public nuisance caused by it.

PhD researcher Rosa van der Drift compared the sale prices of 6,233 Amsterdam homes between 2015 and 2023, taking account of factors such as size and condition. Homes within 500 metres of the shop sold for 4.88% less on average, or about €41,000.

Within 70 metres, the gap widened to 11.4%. The study does not establish any correlation with causation.

Old licence
The court case was made by a group of residents against the city council, not the business. They argue the council did not properly weigh their interests when it granted Fabel Friet an operating licence, and want the licence withdrawn or its conditions tightened.

In 2024, a judge suspended a council rule limiting the queue to 10 people after Fabel Friet called it unworkable.

On Tuesday, one resident told the court there were people eating chips outside “every day, from 11 in the morning until 9 in the evening”, AT5 reported. The residents’ lawyer said a serious accident on the crowded bridge was only a matter of time.

The owners told the court their crowd managers keep the queue safe, the street is cleaned 4 times a day and crowds are down 23% since they opened other branches. For a while they hired a falcon 3 times a week to scare off the gulls, but stopped when residents began using it as evidence against them.

A representative of mayor Femke Halsema acknowledged that the old licence had not been effective enough, and said stricter conditions had been added to the current one about 6 months ago. “It is complicated,” the representative said, according to AT5. “You are so successful, is that not allowed?”

The judge urged both sides to find common ground, reminding the residents of the Dutch saying that a good neighbour is better than a distant friend. She will rule within 6 weeks, but only on the old licence, because objections to the current licence have yet to be decided.

item.title: Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings
item.description:
Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after announcing it, so that fewer people with modest savings are impacted.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen, of the right-wing liberal VVD, made the commitment in parliament on Thursday after MPs from both opposition and coalition parties attacked the plan.

“I have discussed this with the prime minister and with the coalition,” the Financieel Dagblad reported him as saying. “We are prepared to make changes. There will be a proposal to spare small savers.”

Under the plan presented on Tuesday, people would pay 36% tax on returns above €1,000 a year from 2028, down from €1,800 in the earlier version of the reform. Heinen also said he still believed the plan would exempt couples with up to €100,000 in savings.

No funding yet
The minister said he did not yet know how the cabinet would make up the shortfall. Small savers were the main source of funding for the box 3 overhaul, which reports say could cost up to €20 billion.

“We don’t have many levers to pull,” Heinen said. “And every choice you make is enormously complicated.”

The cabinet will send the bill to the Council of State, the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, without an alternative source of funding. Heinen said he would come up with proposals by October 12, when MPs debate the cabinet’s annual package of tax changes.

He also said he would look again at a temporary measure for next year, which would cut the tax-free allowance from €59,357 to €30,846 per person and raise the tax rate. You can find out more about how the changes would affect you in our box 3 explainer.

item.title: Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
item.description:
Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch royal family, the House of Orange-Nassau, earned an estimated €576 million from slavery, mostly in the former Dutch East Indies, according to a new investigation into the monarchy.

The research was commissioned by king Willem-Alexander, who granted access to the royal archives and funded the inquiry.

“All stadtholders, kings, and queens, at least up to and including Wilhelmina, were convinced of the legitimacy of colonialism and its importance for the Netherlands,” lead researcher Gert Oostindie said during a ceremony on Friday to present the findings.

The 2,000 page report has been published into five books and was presented to the king. Willem-Alexander described the conclusions as “heartbreaking and confronting” during the gathering at the Academy Building in Leiden.

“I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future to the best of my ability,” he said.

According to the research, the royals earned very little from the transatlantic slave trade, not because they were opposed but because they were unsuccessful.

Oostindie’s work found that while monarchs voiced support for the institution, few had a direct impact on policy.

Only King William I, who was in power from 1813 to 1840, had a direct hand in colonial slavery. Prior to that, leaders left it to the States General, the country’s early administrative assembly, or to the powerful Dutch East India Company (VOC).

After the reign of William I, monarchs were forced to share power with an increasingly important parliament, which made most of the policy decisions.

Willem-Alexander asked Oostindie, a former professor of colonial history, to conduct the investigation in 2022. Sixty researchers were involved in the nearly four year project.

In 2023, the king formally apologised for the Netherlands’ slave trading history during an annual commemoration for the abolition of the practice.

The monarch also stopped using a ceremonial golden coach which has repeatedly come under fire for a painted panel that depicts scenes of colonialism.

Research by the home affairs ministry in 2023 came to a similar conclusion. That study, carried out following a 2021 parliamentary motion, involved some 30 academics and historians and was published as the book Staat en slavernij (State and slavery).

item.title: Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
item.description:
Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Rivers in the east of the Netherlands have fallen so low that the authorities can no longer measure whether ships can pass safely, leaving skippers to decide for themselves whether or not to sail and risk getting stranded.

Rijkswaterstaat, the transport ministry department that manages the waterways, told broadcaster NOS its survey boats can no longer reach the shallowest stretches of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal.

In certain places the channel is less than 125cm deep, leaving only three agency boats that are shallow enough, but they are also needed in other regions.

Without them, Rijkswaterstaat cannot publish its daily shipping readings of the depths, which barge operators use to avoid getting stranded. Commercial firms collect and sell similar data, but not every skipper has or can pay for a subscription.

Transport under pressure
“This is very worrying,” Fiona Oomen, of inland shipping association Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland, told NOS. “All transport is under pressure, on the roads and on the waterways. What if the water drops even further? Where is everything supposed to go?”

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, is now around 545 cubic metres per second. That is well below the record low of 614 set in August.

Last weekend a Dutch cruise ship carrying 140 passengers became stuck at Cologne as the Rhine dropped to new lows in Germany.

On the IJssel, a one-way system imposed last week has forced some vessels to take a detour of up to 300km.

Freight carried on Dutch waterways fell by 19% in August, according to CBS figures, with cross-border traffic with Germany worst hit.

The infrastructure ministry lifted the national water shortage in early September, but warned that river levels could stay low until the end of the year. The cabinet has ruled out compensation for businesses hit by the drought.

Rain needed
Rijkswaterstaat could not say how long the situation would last. “We need rain in the catchment area,” a spokesman told NOS, adding that it would have to fall mainly outside the Netherlands. Current forecasts suggest the flow will not get worse, but will not improve much either.

He warned that a different problem would follow. “When it’s over, we get the next problem,” he said. “Then we’ll have high water again.” The North Sea is currently exceptionally warm, which could mean a very wet autumn.

item.title: Inflation rate rose slightly in August
item.description:
Inflation rate rose slightly in August

October 2, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

New numbers from the Dutch statistics agency CBS show  the inflation rate rose slightly in August.

The preliminary estimate from the Central Agency for Statistics shows a 0.1% rise from August, putting September’s inflation rate at 3.4%.

The final numbers will be released on October 13.

Fuel and energy prices account for most of the increase. The cost of petrol and gas for heating is was up 13.9% in September over the same month the year before.

Grocery prices, however, have dropped slightly for the second month in a row. Food staples were down 1.3% over the year before, after dropping 0.5% in August.
